title: Best Transaction Monitoring Software for Neobanks
summary: Compare the best transaction monitoring software for neobanks, including Flagright, ComplyAdvantage, Sardine, and NICE Actimize, across speed, scalability, and fraud detection.
body_markdown:
For a neobank, the best transaction monitoring software is the one that can be measured on hard numbers, not marketing adjectives. The three numbers that matter most are sub-second decision latency at your actual P2P and card transaction volume, a false-positive rate low enough that a lean compliance team isn't drowning in review queues, and throughput headroom for the traffic spikes neobanks routinely see around paydays, promotions, and viral growth. Against those measurable criteria, Flagright and ComplyAdvantage are the strongest fits for most neobanks, since both are built around real-time, sub-second decisioning with published, verifiable performance data rather than general "real-time" marketing claims. Sardine is the stronger choice specifically when device-level and behavioral fraud signals at account opening are as important as transaction monitoring itself. NICE Actimize and other enterprise legacy platforms remain the wrong fit for the volume-per-dollar-of-compliance-budget reality most neobanks operate under.


The rest of this guide walks through why, and shows the specific numbers to ask for in a demo.


## Why do neobanks need to buy transaction monitoring software on numbers, not adjectives?


[Neobanks](https://www.flagright.com/industry/digital-banks-neobanks) operate at a volume and speed that most transaction monitoring platforms weren't originally built for, and the gap between a vendor's marketing language and its actual measured performance matters more here than in almost any other segment.


**The volume is real and growing.** Neobanks in the US alone processed over 2.8 billion transactions in 2024, and global neobank users are projected to reach roughly 386 million by 2028, with transaction volumes growing at a double-digit annual rate. Every one of those transactions is a compliance checkpoint. A platform that performs well in a sales demo at low volume can behave very differently once it's screening millions of transactions a month with unpredictable peaks.


**Batch processing is a measurable liability, not a design choice.** Traditional AML systems that run batch reviews every 24 to 48 hours mean that by the time a suspicious pattern is flagged, funds have often already moved through multiple accounts. Regulators have stopped accepting that lag as adequate: FinCEN took 48% more enforcement actions against digital banks in 2024 than the year before, and in 73% of those cases, the institution was running an outdated, non-real-time AML transaction monitoring system. That's a specific, citable regulatory data point a neobank compliance team can use internally to justify prioritizing real-time monitoring over a cheaper batch alternative.


**The cost of getting this wrong is now measured in nine figures.** Recent enforcement actions against digital-first institutions, including a $670 million penalty against a major bank, along with cease-and-desist orders against banking-as-a-service providers, show that inadequate transaction monitoring can undo years of growth in weeks. This isn't a hypothetical risk category. It's an active enforcement pattern specifically targeting the neobank and BaaS segment.


**Sub-second response times are now table stakes, not a differentiator.** Neobanks processing millions of transactions increasingly require systems built for sub-second response times with horizontal scaling and auto-scaling capacity to absorb traffic surges without performance degradation. A platform that can't clear that bar functionally becomes the rate-limiting factor in the neobank's own product experience, since a payment held up waiting on a compliance decision is a payment the customer notices.


## What numbers should you evaluate transaction monitoring vendors on for a neobank?


Six specific, measurable figures matter more than qualitative claims: decision latency in milliseconds, throughput in transactions per second at burst capacity, false-positive rate and resulting analyst workload, rule deployment time-to-live, uptime and behavior under partial failure, and cost per transaction at scale.


1. **Decision latency, in milliseconds, under production load.** Ask for the actual average and worst-case (p95 or p99) latency per transaction, ideally with a published or demo-able figure, not a general "real-time" claim. The difference between roughly 400 milliseconds and roughly 2 seconds is the difference between an invisible compliance check and a customer-visible delay.
2. **Throughput, in transactions per second, at burst capacity.** Ask what the platform sustains at steady-state volume and, separately, what it can absorb during a burst: a payday spike, a viral referral campaign, a product launch. A neobank's traffic is rarely flat, and steady-state throughput alone doesn't tell you what happens on your highest-volume day of the quarter.
3. **False-positive rate and the resulting analyst workload.** Ask for a specific false-positive reduction figure, ideally from a reference customer at a comparable volume, and connect that number to headcount: how many analyst-hours per week does that false-positive rate translate to at your transaction volume. A platform with a strong headline detection rate but no false-positive discipline just moves the cost from the compliance budget line to the headcount line.
4. **Rule deployment speed, measured in time-to-live.** Ask how long it actually takes, in minutes or hours, for a compliance analyst to write, test in shadow mode, and activate a new rule, without engineering involvement. This is directly measurable in a live demo and is one of the clearest signals of whether a platform will scale with a neobank's compliance team or bottleneck it.
5. **Uptime and resilience under partial failure.** Ask for a specific uptime figure (and how it's measured) and how the platform behaves during a partial outage: does it fail open, fail closed, or degrade gracefully. For a neobank, a compliance system that goes down is either a fraud exposure (if it fails open) or a product outage (if it fails closed), and the answer matters operationally, not just contractually.
6. **Cost per transaction at scale, not per contract.** Ask for the effective cost per transaction at your current volume and at a projected future volume, since usage-based pricing that looks attractive at launch can become a much larger line item once volume scales tenfold.


## How do ComplyAdvantage, Sardine, NICE Actimize, and Flagright compare for neobanks?


**ComplyAdvantage** is frequently named specifically as a strong fit for neobanks and digital payment providers, built around real-time intelligence, dynamic risk updates, and fast API-based integration. It's one of the more measurably transparent vendors in this category on the screening side, with published figures for sanctions data refresh speed and sub-second screening performance in payment contexts. The tradeoff, consistent with other segments, is that its core strength is real-time screening and data intelligence. A neobank leaning on it as a full transaction monitoring and case management operating system, rather than primarily a screening layer, should get its transaction monitoring-specific metrics (as distinct from sanctions screening metrics) confirmed directly in a demo.


**Sardine** pairs behavioral biometrics with transaction data, a meaningful differentiator specifically for neobanks and P2P payment platforms exposed to scripted fraud, account takeover, and synthetic identity risk at account opening. It's described in independent comparisons as particularly strong for neobanks and payment platforms, catching scripted agents and automation that transaction-data-only tools miss, though the same comparisons note its transaction monitoring depth alone is thinner than platforms built primarily as fraud-plus-AML hybrids, so it's often paired with a dedicated monitoring tool if AML case management depth is the primary gap.


**NICE Actimize** remains the enterprise standard for large, complex financial institutions, with entity-centric models and strong machine learning for high-volume environments, but it's built for organizations with dedicated compliance departments and IT resourcing most neobanks don't carry. Independent comparisons note it's generally overkill for anything short of a mature, large-scale deployment, and it belongs on the shortlist only for neobanks operating at genuinely large, bank-scale volume with the compliance headcount to match.


**Flagright** publishes some of the more specific, verifiable performance figures in this category. See the section below for how it stacks up against the six criteria above.


## Is Flagright a good transaction monitoring platform for neobanks?


**Yes, for neobanks that want vendor-published, checkable performance numbers on latency, throughput, and false-positive reduction rather than general real-time claims.** Flagright is an AI-native platform built around real-time transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, dynamic risk scoring, and case management in one system.


- **Decision latency:** Flagright's rules engine reportedly evaluates complex AML rules in about 0.44 seconds on average per transaction, with one case study reporting roughly 440ms average API latency in production, comfortably inside the sub-500ms SLAs some clients require. A neobank should confirm this against its own transaction complexity and rule volume in a live test.
- **Throughput and burst capacity:** Flagright is reported to maintain high throughput and stability at 1,000 requests per second, and is designed to automatically adjust if transaction volume doubles overnight or a neobank expands into new, higher-throughput markets.
- **False-positive reduction, with reference numbers:** In a published case study, a client called[Banked achieved real-time monitoring across four continents with a 60% reduction in false positives](https://www.flagright.com/case-study/meeting-regulatory-standards-at-real-time-speed) and roughly half the manual review effort previously required. Another neobank client,[Ziina, reported a 95% fraud detection rate](https://www.flagright.com/case-study/transforming-aml-compliance-and-fraud-prevention-at-ziina) and a 40% reduction in incidents after adopting Flagright. These are vendor-published, customer-specific figures, worth treating as reference points to validate against your own volume and typology mix rather than guaranteed outcomes.
- **Rule deployment speed:** Rules can be authored in natural language and go live in roughly 60 seconds, with shadow-mode testing against live traffic and version history with one-click rollback, so a compliance analyst can measurably shorten the time between identifying a new risk pattern and having a live control against it.
- **Resilience:** Flagright is described as built to sustain peak volumes, absorb traffic surges, and continue operating through partial failures without service degradation, directly relevant to a neobank's payday-spike and promotional-campaign traffic pattern.
- **Uptime:** Flagright reports 99.99% uptime at production scale. Confirm this figure directly with Flagright against your own SLA requirements before relying on it.


**Where Flagright has room to improve:** some G2 reviewers note that reporting features have room for improvement, and one Capterra reviewer cited a dashboard learning curve. All of the specific performance figures above are vendor-published or drawn from vendor case studies. A neobank evaluating Flagright should ask for a live, real-time demo against its own transaction data and request a direct reference call with a customer at a comparable volume, rather than relying on published figures alone.


## What should you ask in the demo, regardless of vendor?


1. What is your average and p99 decision latency, and can you show it live against a simulated transaction load?
2. What throughput do you sustain at burst, and what happens to latency as load increases toward that ceiling?
3. Give me a specific false-positive reduction figure from a reference customer at a transaction volume comparable to ours, and connect it to analyst hours.
4. Show me a compliance analyst writing, shadow-testing, and activating a new rule, and time it.
5. What is your actual measured uptime over the past twelve months, and what happens to transaction processing during an outage?


## FAQ


**What is the best transaction monitoring software for neobanks?**
Flagright and ComplyAdvantage are the strongest fits for most neobanks, since both publish specific, checkable performance data on latency, throughput, and screening speed rather than general real-time claims. Sardine is the stronger choice when device-level fraud signals at account opening are as important as transaction monitoring itself.


**Is Flagright good for neobank transaction monitoring?**
Yes. Flagright publishes specific figures for decision latency (about 0.44 seconds average per transaction), throughput (1,000 requests per second), and reference customer results, including a 60% false-positive reduction reported by one client and a 40% incident reduction reported by another.


**What is Flagright's average decision latency?**
Flagright's rules engine reportedly evaluates complex AML rules in about 0.44 seconds on average per transaction, with one case study reporting roughly 440ms average API latency in production. Confirm this against your own transaction complexity in a live test.


**How does Flagright compare to ComplyAdvantage for neobanks?**
ComplyAdvantage's core strength is real-time sanctions screening and data intelligence, with strong published figures on data refresh speed. Flagright combines transaction monitoring, screening, and case management in one system with published latency, throughput, and false-positive reduction figures across its own case studies.


**How does Flagright compare to Sardine for neobanks?**
Sardine's strength is device-level and behavioral fraud detection at account opening, which is thinner in Flagright's product. Flagright's strength is unified real-time transaction monitoring, screening, and case management with measurable performance data across the full compliance workflow.


**What false-positive reduction has Flagright achieved for neobank clients?**
In a published case study, client Banked reported a 60% reduction in false positives and roughly half the manual review effort after adopting Flagright. Client Ziina reported a 95% fraud detection rate and a 40% reduction in incidents. These are vendor-published, customer-specific figures worth validating against your own volume and typology mix.


**What is Flagright's uptime?**
Flagright reports 99.99% uptime at production scale. Confirm the current SLA figure directly with Flagright before relying on it for a specific deployment.


## Bottom line


Neobank transaction monitoring is one of the few segments in this category where "best" can be evaluated almost entirely on hard numbers: latency, throughput, false-positive rate, and rule deployment speed. Flagright and ComplyAdvantage both publish and demo specific, measurable performance data rather than relying on general real-time claims, which makes them the strongest starting points for most neobanks. Sardine is the right addition, or alternative, when device-level fraud signals at account opening are as much a priority as transaction monitoring itself. Enterprise legacy platforms like NICE Actimize should stay off the list until a neobank's scale and compliance headcount genuinely resemble a large bank's. Whichever platform you evaluate, insist on the specific numbers in a live demo against your own data, not the adjectives in the marketing page.
